```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)

# Must match EXPERIMENT.id in experiment.js, and the --experiment you passed to the export.
# Phase 2 runs under its own id, so its data never mix with Phase 1's.
experiment_id        <- "jara-ettinger2021-phase1"
experiment_id_phase2 <- "jara-ettinger2021-phase2"
```

```{r}
#| label: original-study
#| include: false
# The original study's numbers, entered once and used by the power analysis, the Key
# statistics table, and the side-by-side figures. 
#
# Jara-Ettinger & Rubio-Fernandez (2021), Experiment 1 (N = 60): Each participant's performance
# on the belief inference task was compared against a theory of mind model (Model A) and a deductive model (Model B)
# The subject-level difference is tested with a paired t test. (Page 4, Paragraph 4)
original <- list(
  n = 60,   # number of participants in the paired test
  t = 5.43,    # paired t statistic, Model A vs Model B
  mean_diff = 0.24 # mean difference between correlation of Model A and Model B
)
original_dz <- original$t / sqrt(original$n)
```

# Key statistics

```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (shared by Phase 1 and Phase 2)"

# Load one phase's exported data and apply the exclusion rule. Returns NULL if that phase
# has not been exported yet, which is how every section below knows to skip itself.
# min_referent_r: Phase 2's added exclusion (Changes from Phase 1, row 2): keep only participants
# whose referent correlation with the ToM model is above this value. NULL (Phase 1) skips it.
read_phase <- function(id, min_referent_r = NULL) {
  dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", id)
  if (!all(file.exists(file.path(dir, c("participants.csv", "trials.csv"))))) return(NULL)
  participants <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "participants.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  trials       <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "trials.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  errors_path  <- file.path(dir, "errors.csv")
  errors <- if (file.exists(errors_path)) read_csv(errors_path, show_col_types = FALSE) else tibble()

  complete <- participants |> filter(completed)

  # Exclusion rule: analyze everyone who finished the study and has all 14 trials saved.
  # The original experiment data contain only complete sessions and report no exclusions.
  n_main <- trials |>
    filter(task == "trial") |>
    count(participant_id, name = "n_main_trials")
  keep <- complete |>
    left_join(n_main, by = "participant_id") |>
    filter(n_main_trials %in% 14)

  if (!is.null(min_referent_r)) {
    referent_ok <- trials |>
      filter(task == "trial", participant_id %in% keep$participant_id) |>
      select(participant_id, TrialId = trial_id,
             lref_x = ref_a_x, lref_y = ref_a_y, rref_x = ref_b_x, rref_y = ref_b_y) |>
      pivot_longer(lref_x:rref_y, names_to = "variable", values_to = "response") |>
      left_join(model_predictions, by = c("TrialId", "variable")) |>
      group_by(participant_id) |>
      summarise(referent_r = suppressWarnings(score_fit(response, ToM)), .groups = "drop") |>
      filter(referent_r > min_referent_r)
    keep <- keep |> semi_join(referent_ok, by = "participant_id")
  }

  list(participants = participants, trials = trials, errors = errors,
       complete = complete, keep = keep)
}

# Model predictions for the 28 trials, from the authors' OSF archive (osf.io/h8qfy,
# ProcessedData/Exp1_Model.csv): "ToM" is Model A, "Deductive" is Model B. Same coordinates as
# the trackpads: x = probability of the right column, y = probability of the bottom row;
# lref = display A, rref = display B, cg = blind spot.
model_predictions <- read_csv(file.path("..", "data", "original", "Exp1_Model.csv"),
                              show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  pivot_longer(lref_x:cg_y, names_to = "variable") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = value)

# How well one participant's responses fit one model: as in the original's subject-level
# analysis (Exp1_AnalyzeResults.R), the correlation across that participant's 14 trials
# between their trackpad positions (x and y, so 28 values) and the model's predictions.
score_fit <- function(response, prediction) cor(response, prediction, use = "complete.obs")

# Each analyzed participant's fit to Model A and Model B, and the difference (A - B), for
# belief (blind spot) inferences, the cg_x and cg_y trackpad. Responses are already in the
# model's orientation (experiment.js undoes the rotation and left/right swap). Participants
# whose fit can't be computed (e.g. the blind-spot marker never moved) are dropped here.
# Run on the original participants' data, this reproduces the paper: 0.586 vs 0.350, t(59) = 5.43.
participant_scores <- function(d) {
  d$trials |>
    filter(task == "trial", participant_id %in% d$keep$participant_id) |>
    select(participant_id, TrialId = trial_id, cg_x, cg_y) |>
    pivot_longer(c(cg_x, cg_y), names_to = "variable", values_to = "response") |>
    left_join(model_predictions, by = c("TrialId", "variable")) |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(score_a = suppressWarnings(score_fit(response, ToM)),
              score_b = suppressWarnings(score_fit(response, Deductive)),
              .groups = "drop") |>
    filter(!is.na(score_a), !is.na(score_b)) |>
    mutate(diff = score_a - score_b)
}

# Per-participant fits for belief (cg) and referent (lref, rref) inferences separately, from
# responses in long form (participant_id, TrialId, variable, response). Used by the
# participant-level figures, which put the original participants next to ours. For belief
# inferences this gives the same scores as participant_scores().
fits_by_type <- function(long) {
  long |>
    mutate(type = if_else(startsWith(variable, "cg"), "Belief", "Referent")) |>
    left_join(model_predictions, by = c("TrialId", "variable")) |>
    group_by(participant_id, type) |>
    summarise(score_a = suppressWarnings(score_fit(response, ToM)),
              score_b = suppressWarnings(score_fit(response, Deductive)),
              .groups = "drop") |>
    filter(!is.na(score_a), !is.na(score_b)) |>
    mutate(diff = score_a - score_b)
}

replication_long <- function(d) {
  d$trials |>
    filter(task == "trial", participant_id %in% d$keep$participant_id) |>
    select(participant_id, TrialId = trial_id, cg_x, cg_y,
           lref_x = ref_a_x, lref_y = ref_a_y, rref_x = ref_b_x, rref_y = ref_b_y) |>
    pivot_longer(cg_x:rref_y, names_to = "variable", values_to = "response")
}
replication_fits <- function(d) fits_by_type(replication_long(d))

# The original participants' responses, from the authors' OSF archive (osf.io/h8qfy,
# ProcessedData/Exp1_Participants.csv), already in the model's coordinates. Scored this way
# they reproduce the paper's subject-level results: belief 0.586 vs 0.350 (45 of 60 fit
# Model A better), referent 0.933 vs 0.933.
original_long <- read_csv(file.path("..", "data", "original", "Exp1_Participants.csv"),
                          show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(participant_id = UserId, TrialId, cg_x:rref_y) |>
  pivot_longer(cg_x:rref_y, names_to = "variable", values_to = "response")
original_fits <- fits_by_type(original_long)

# Item-level ("collapsed") analysis, as in the original's Exp1_AnalyzeResults.R (osf.io/h8qfy,
# AnalysisFiles): average all participants' responses for each trial and trackpad coordinate
# (28 trials x 6 = 168 values, 56 belief and 112 referent), then correlate those averages with
# each model. CIs are basic bootstraps over items with 10,000 resamples and the original's
# seeds. On the original data this reproduces the paper's estimates exactly (belief r = 0.947
# ToM vs 0.561 deductive, difference 0.386; referent 0.994 vs 0.993) and its CIs to within
# about 0.005 (the original draws the lower and upper bound from separate bootstrap runs).
item_means <- function(long) {
  long |>
    group_by(TrialId, variable) |>
    summarise(human = mean(response, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    left_join(model_predictions, by = c("TrialId", "variable")) |>
    mutate(type = if_else(startsWith(variable, "cg"), "Belief", "Referent"))
}

boot_basic <- function(data, stat, seed, R = 10000) {
  set.seed(seed)
  b <- boot::boot(data, stat, R = R)
  ci <- boot::boot.ci(b, type = "basic")$basic[4:5]
  tibble(estimate = b$t0, ci_low = ci[1], ci_high = ci[2])
}

# r with each model, by inference type and pooled over both types.
item_corrs <- function(items) {
  r_with <- function(model) function(d, i) cor(d$human[i], d[[model]][i])
  by_type <- items |> mutate(group = type)
  pooled  <- items |> mutate(group = "Overall")
  bind_rows(by_type, pooled) |>
    group_by(group) |>
    reframe(bind_rows(boot_basic(pick(everything()), r_with("ToM"), 23754) |> mutate(model = "ToM model"),
                      boot_basic(pick(everything()), r_with("Deductive"), 23754) |> mutate(model = "Deductive model"))) |>
    rename(type = group)
}

# ToM r minus deductive r over the same items, by inference type.
item_diff <- function(items) {
  r_diff <- function(d, i) cor(d$ToM[i], d$human[i]) - cor(d$Deductive[i], d$human[i])
  items |> group_by(type) |> reframe(boot_basic(pick(everything()), r_diff, 7582))
}

# The key statistic: mean paired difference (Model A minus Model B) with a 95% CI, the
# paired t test, and d_z. NULL until at least two participants have scores.
paired_test <- function(scores) {
  if (is.null(scores) || nrow(scores) < 2) return(NULL)
  tt <- t.test(scores$score_a, scores$score_b, paired = TRUE)
  tibble(N = nrow(scores),
         estimate  = unname(tt$estimate),
         ci_low    = tt$conf.int[1], ci_high = tt$conf.int[2],
         statistic = unname(tt$statistic), df = unname(tt$parameter), p = tt$p.value,
         d_z       = mean(scores$diff) / sd(scores$diff))
}

# The original study's paired difference and 95% CI, rebuilt from its reported mean
# difference, paired t, and N, in the same shape paired_test() returns.
original_paired <- function(o) {
  df   <- o$n - 1
  se   <- abs(o$mean_diff / o$t)
  half <- qt(0.975, df) * se
  tibble(N = o$n, estimate = o$mean_diff,
         ci_low = o$mean_diff - half, ci_high = o$mean_diff + half,
         statistic = o$t, df = df, p = 2 * pt(-abs(o$t), df),
         d_z = o$t / sqrt(o$n))
}

# Side-by-side figure: each study's paired difference with its 95% CI, in the order given.
comparison_plot <- function(...) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, is.null)]
  df <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y)) |>
    mutate(Study = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)), label = sprintf("n = %d", N))
  cols <- setNames(c("grey55", "#1E6E76", "#B8792A")[seq_along(studies)], names(studies))
  ggplot(df, aes(x = Study, y = estimate, colour = Study)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
    geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = ci_low, ymax = ci_high), size = 0.6) +
    geom_text(aes(y = ci_high, label = label), vjust = -0.8, size = 3, colour = "grey30") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = cols, guide = "none") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Difference in correlation with \nToM and deductive models per-participant") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
}

comparison_plot_with_points <- function(..., points = list()) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, is.null)]
  df <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y)) |>
    mutate(Study = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)), label = sprintf("n = %d", N))
  cols <- setNames(c("grey55", "#1E6E76", "#B8792A")[seq_along(studies)], names(studies))

  points <- points[!map_lgl(points, is.null) & names(points) %in% names(studies)]
  point_layer <- NULL
  if (length(points) > 0) {
    pts_df <- imap_dfr(points, ~ tibble(Study = .y, diff = .x$diff)) |>
      mutate(Study = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)))
    point_layer <- geom_point(data = pts_df, aes(y = diff),
                              position = position_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, seed = 251),
                              alpha = 0.35, size = 5)
  }

  ggplot(df, aes(x = Study, y = estimate, colour = Study)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
    point_layer +
    geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = ci_low, ymax = ci_high), size = 1.5, linewidth = 1.5) +
    geom_text(aes(y = Inf, label = label), vjust = 1.5, size = 10, colour = "grey30") +
    # headroom above the highest point for the n labels
    scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.15))) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = cols, guide = "none") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Difference in correlation with \nToM and deductive models per-participant") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 28) +
    theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 24))
}

phase1 <- read_phase(experiment_id)
phase2 <- read_phase(experiment_id_phase2, min_referent_r = 0.8)
have_data   <- !is.null(phase1)
have_phase2 <- !is.null(phase2)
```

```{r}
#| label: key-stats
#| echo: false
fmt_row <- function(study, r) {
  if (is.null(r)) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = "", `Difference (A − B)` = "not yet collected",
                  `95% CI` = "", `t (df)` = "", p = "", `d_z` = ""))
  }
  tibble(Study = study, N = as.character(r$N),
         `Difference (A − B)` = sprintf("%.3f", r$estimate),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", r$ci_low, r$ci_high),
         `t (df)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.0f)", r$statistic, r$df),
         p = format.pval(r$p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001),
         `d_z` = sprintf("%.2f", r$d_z))
}
bind_rows(
  fmt_row("Original", original_paired(original)),
  fmt_row("Phase 1: replication", if (have_data) paired_test(participant_scores(phase1))),
  fmt_row("Phase 2: extension", if (have_phase2) paired_test(participant_scores(phase2)))
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrllllr",
               caption = "Key comparison: mean per-participant difference in fit to Model A minus Model B, paired t test.")
```

# Phase 1: Replication

## Introduction
In this project, I tried to replicate Experiment 1 of Jara-Ettinger & Rubio-Fernandez (2021). The original study found that adults can infer what information speakers know about objects based on the specificity of the language they use to refer to them. In Experiment 1, participants were shown four shapes on a screen and then told that speakers could not see one of the four objects and to guess what the speaker was referring to and what the speaker's blind spot was. They found that adults' predictions about which of the four shapes speakers did not know was better predicted by a theory of mind model that inferred speakers' knowledge from the specificity of their reference, than a deductive model that did not. The key statistic I aimed to replicate was that participants' belief predictions were better predicted by the theory of mind model compared to the deductive model (*t*(59) = 5.43, *p* < 0.0001 by paired *t* test) 

This finding mattered to me since I am interested in thinking about frameworks to use to understand how children reason about speaker beliefs to learn words. In pursuit of that goal, I initially planeed to extend this study by replacing the speaker object reference with a 2-3 sentence long conversational segment from CHILDES, a naturalistic corpus of what children hear, and replaced the objects with real-world objects that could be referred to across these segments.

## Methods

### Power analysis

The original effect size found was 0.70. Details about the number of participants required to detect that effect with different amounts of power are detailed below.

```{r}
#| label: power
power_rows <- map_dfr(c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95), function(pw) {
  n <- power.t.test(delta = original_dz, sd = 1, power = pw,
                    sig.level = 0.05, type = "paired")$n
  tibble(power = scales::percent(pw), n = ceiling(n))
})

two_and_half <- ceiling(2.5 * original$n)

knitr::kable(power_rows, col.names = c("Power", "N participants"),
             caption = sprintf(
               "Participants needed to detect the original Model A vs Model B difference (d_z = %.2f), paired t test, two-sided alpha = .05.",
               original_dz))
```

For comparison, 2.5 times the original sample would be `r two_and_half[1]` in total. I chose a sample size of 20 to be able to detect the original effect size with at least 80% power.

### Planned sample

I planned to collect a sample size of 20. Those participants were required to be US residents on Prolific who were fluent in English and 18 or older. I collected data until 20 participants passed the exclusion criteria below.

### Materials

Tutorial: "Participants first read a brief tutorial and had to complete a small questionnaire to ensure they
read the instructions. See our OSF site for screenshots of the tutorial, inclusion
questionnaire, and test screen." Instructions pages 6, 7, 8, and 9 were updated to remove the 'Continue' button in the screenshots of the study to avoid confusion with the JS-Psych version of the 'Continue' button used that looks slightly different. The inclusion questionnaire was adapted into JS-Psych but had the same list of questions.

Shapes: "Stimuli consisted of 28 trials. Each trial in turn consisted of two 2 × 2 grids with four colored geometrical shapes and a definite description of one of them. Displays were created by combining 4 shapes (circle, square, triangle and star) in 4 colors (red, green, blue and yellow). We generated 4 possible conditions for each display by crossing the
presence or absence of a color adjective in the target description with the presence or absence of
a contrast shape in the display" The original authors provided information about each of the 28 trials (display combinations and utterance) on OSF that were used to design the stimuli for this study. Since the original authors did not provide the shapes themselves, I recreated these shapes as SVG objects based on how these objects appeared in the test screen screenshot. 

### Procedure

Participants first consented to participating in the study. Then, participants had to "read a brief tutorial and had to complete a small questionnaire to ensure they read the instructions. Participants who got at least one question wrong were redirected to the beginning of the tutorial and only participants who responded to all questions correctly were
allowed to participate in the study." 

Each participant saw 14 trials as part of the study. "Stimuli were randomly split into two subsets of 14 trials, and participants were presented with only one of the two lists" "Each trial in turn consisted of two 2 × 2 grids with four colored geometrical shapes and a definite description of one of them." "In each trial, participants were told that the speaker intended to refer to only one of the corners and that the speaker could not see one of the four corners. Participants were also told that the speaker could not see the same corner in each display. The speaker’s choice of referential expression to single out the target was written above each display. Trial order was randomized across participants. The pairs of displays were randomly ordered and rotated in each trial. In each trial, participants were presented with three 'trackpads,' each with a circle that the participants could position anywhere they wished. Participants had to input their belief about the referent in each display in the first two trackpads and their beliefs about the blind spot in the third trackpad." 

After the trials, participants were asked how old they were, to match the demographic data collected in the original study. On the next screen, participants were asked to optionally provide any comments they have. Finally, participants were shown a debrief screen where the purpose of the experiment is explained and it is disclosed that the speaker was simulated. 

The study took 20 minutes in total.

### Analysis plan

**Key analysis of interest.** Participants' performance on the belief task has a higher correlation with a theory-of-mind model as compared to a deductive model, tested with a paired t-test comparing the per-participant correlation difference. The effect size is the mean difference divided by the standard deviation of the differences, with a 95% confidence interval.

**Exclusions.** Participants will be excluded if they do not complete the study or if a model correlation score cannot be computed. Since the original experiment only contained participants with complete data, I added the first criterion to ensure that standard was matched. A model correlation score can always be computed unless a participant does not move the blind-spot marker at least once, so I added the second criterion to exclude participants who did not successfully comprehend the task and on whose data the key analysis of interest cannot be performed.   

### Differences from the original study

| Aspect | Original study | This replication | Expected to matter? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | Adults recruited on Amazon Mechanical Turk | Adults recruited on Prolific residing in the United States who speak English | Unlikely, the task uses shapes and no context-specific items and both samples are collected online. |
| Instructions | 'Continue' button in task design screenshot | No 'Continue' button in task design screenshot | Unlikely. The presence of the button is not relevant to understanding of the task design. |
| Exclusion criteria | None | Participants are excluded if they do not complete the study or if a model correlation score cannot be computed. | Unlikely, since all of the participants in the original sample had complete data and because only participants who do not move the blind-spot marker at all, indicating lack of comprehension of the study design, will have data that cannot be compared to the model. |
| Additional tasks | None | Participants are asked to provide their age and any additional comments | Unlikely. These tasks are only asked to be completed after the participant completes the experimental trials. |

```{r}
#| label: funnel

funnel_levels <- c("Started", "Completed", "Passed exclusion criteria", "Model fit computable")
# participant_scores() drops anyone whose fit to either model is NA (e.g. the blind-spot

bind_rows(
  participants |> mutate(step = "Started"),
  complete     |> mutate(step = "Completed"),
  keep         |> mutate(step = "Passed exclusion criteria"),
  scored       |> mutate(step = "Model fit computable")
) |>
  mutate(step = factor(step, levels = funnel_levels)) |>
  count(step, condition, .drop = FALSE) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(Total = rowSums(across(-step))) |>
  rename(Step = step) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Participants at each step, by trial list. Differences between lists in attrition or exclusion are a threat to validity and should be discussed.")
```

## Results

### Data preparation

Data preparation followed the analysis plan.

### Confirmatory analysis

```{r}
#| label: confirmatory
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Belief inferences: each participant's correlation with Model A (ToM) vs Model B (deductive),
# paired t test (original: 0.586 vs 0.350, t(59) = 5.43).
scores <- participant_scores(phase1)
key    <- paired_test(scores)

if (!is.null(key)) {
  print(t.test(scores$score_a, scores$score_b, paired = TRUE))
  scores |>
    summarise(N = n(), `Mean r, Model A (ToM)` = mean(score_a),
              `Mean r, Model B (deductive)` = mean(score_b),
              `Model A fits better` = sum(diff > 0)) |>
    knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Per-participant correlations with each model, belief inferences.")
} else {
  message("Paired t test not run: it needs at least two analysed participants with a computable ",
          "correlation; there are ", nrow(scores), ".")
}
```

### Replication assessment

```{r}
#| label: comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
orig <- original_paired(original)
rep  <- key

if (!is.null(rep)) {
  bind_rows(orig |> mutate(Study = "Original"), rep |> mutate(Study = "Phase 1: replication")) |>
    transmute(Study, N,
              `Difference in r (A − B)` = sprintf("%.2f", estimate),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high),
              d_z = sprintf("%.2f", d_z),
              p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Effect size: mean per-participant difference in correlation with Model A (ToM) and Model B (deductive), belief inferences.")
} else {
  message("Replication effect size not computed yet: need at least two analysed participants.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-verdict

if (!is.null(rep)) {
  excludes_zero <- rep$ci_low > 0 | rep$ci_high < 0
  includes_orig <- orig$estimate >= rep$ci_low & orig$estimate <= rep$ci_high
  cat(sprintf(
    "The replication's 95%% interval %s zero and %s the original estimate of %.2f. ",
    if (excludes_zero) "excludes" else "includes",
    if (includes_orig) "includes" else "does not include",
    orig$estimate))
  cat("These two facts are the starting point for the summary in the Discussion, not the conclusion.\n")
}
```

### Exploratory analyses

In exploratory analyses, I first attempted to replicate all of the statistics and plots reported in the original experiment. I also attempted to use RMSE instead of a simple paired t-test.

```{r}
#| label: exploratory-fit-measures
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Exploratory: the same model comparison with a second fit measure, and restricted to
# participants who passed the comprehension check on their first attempt.
#
# RMSE: root mean squared distance between a participant's trackpad positions and the model's
# predictions, over the same 28 values the correlation uses (lower is a better fit). Unlike r,
# it also penalises responses that track the model's pattern but are shifted or compressed.
# Computed for the same participants and inference types as the correlations.
rmse_by_type <- function(long) {
  long |>
    mutate(type = if_else(startsWith(variable, "cg"), "Belief", "Referent")) |>
    left_join(model_predictions, by = c("TrialId", "variable")) |>
    filter(!is.na(response)) |>
    group_by(participant_id, type) |>
    summarise(rmse_a = sqrt(mean((response - ToM)^2)),
              rmse_b = sqrt(mean((response - Deductive)^2)),
              .groups = "drop")
}
model_fits <- function(long) inner_join(fits_by_type(long), rmse_by_type(long),
                                        by = c("participant_id", "type"))

# Comprehension-check attempts, from the quiz trials (one row per attempt).
quiz_attempts <- trials |>
  filter(task == "quiz") |>
  group_by(participant_id) |>
  summarise(attempts = max(attempt), .groups = "drop")
first_try_ids <- quiz_attempts |> filter(attempts == 1) |> pull(participant_id)

# "estimate [CI], t(df), p" for a paired t test of x - y; blank below two participants.
fmt_paired <- function(x, y) {
  if (length(x) < 2) return("")
  tt <- t.test(x, y, paired = TRUE)
  sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f], t(%.0f) = %.2f, p %s",
          tt$estimate, tt$conf.int[1], tt$conf.int[2], tt$parameter, tt$statistic,
          if (tt$p.value < 0.001) "< .001" else sprintf("= %.3f", tt$p.value))
}

p1_fits   <- model_fits(replication_long(phase1))
orig_fits <- model_fits(original_long)
fit_samples <- list(
  "Original"                              = orig_fits,
  "Phase 1: all analysed"                 = p1_fits,
  "Phase 1: passed check on first try"    = p1_fits |> filter(participant_id %in% first_try_ids),
  "Phase 1: needed more than one try"     = p1_fits |> filter(!participant_id %in% first_try_ids)
)
imap_dfr(fit_samples, ~ .x |>
           group_by(Type = type) |>
           summarise(N = n(),
                     `r: ToM − deductive` = fmt_paired(score_a, score_b),
                     `RMSE ToM` = mean(rmse_a), `RMSE deductive` = mean(rmse_b),
                     # Ordered so that, as for r, a positive difference means ToM fits better.
                     `RMSE: deductive − ToM` = fmt_paired(rmse_b, rmse_a),
                     `ToM better (r / RMSE)` = sprintf("%d / %d", sum(score_a > score_b), sum(rmse_a < rmse_b)),
                     .groups = "drop") |>
           mutate(Sample = .y, .before = 1)) |>
  arrange(Type) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Exploratory: per-participant model comparison by correlation (higher is better) and RMSE (lower is better), for the original, all Phase 1 participants, and Phase 1 split by comprehension-check attempts. Differences are paired, with 95% CIs; positive means the ToM model fits better.")
```

```{r}
                      name = NULL) +
```

I looked at how adding a correlation threshold on the referent task would affect our hypotheses. At around 
```{r}
#| label: fig-referent-threshold
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| fig-cap: "Exploratory: mean per-participant correlation of belief inferences with each model, keeping only Phase 1 participants whose referent correlation with the ToM model is at or above the threshold on the x axis. Ribbons are 95% confidence intervals (shown where at least 5 participants remain); numbers along the bottom give how many participants remain at that threshold. The dashed line marks the 0.8 cutoff planned for Phase 2."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
# Each participant's referent correlation with the ToM model (the two models' referent
# predictions are nearly identical, so the deductive model gives almost the same values),
# joined to their belief correlations with both models.
referent_r <- p1_fits |> filter(type == "Referent") |> select(participant_id, referent_r = score_a)
belief_r   <- p1_fits |> filter(type == "Belief") |> select(participant_id, score_a, score_b)
by_referent <- inner_join(referent_r, belief_r, by = "participant_id")

thresholds <- seq(floor(min(by_referent$referent_r) * 20) / 20, max(by_referent$referent_r), by = 0.01)
threshold_fits <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(th) {
  kept <- filter(by_referent, referent_r >= th)
  pivot_longer(kept, c(score_a, score_b), names_to = "model", values_to = "r") |>
    group_by(model) |>
    summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(r),
              ci_low  = if (n() >= 5) mean(r) - qt(0.975, n() - 1) * sd(r) / sqrt(n()) else NA_real_,
              ci_high = if (n() >= 5) mean(r) + qt(0.975, n() - 1) * sd(r) / sqrt(n()) else NA_real_,
              .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(threshold = th)
}) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = c("score_a", "score_b"),
                        labels = c("ToM model", "Deductive model")))

# Participants remaining, labelled every 0.05 so the labels don't overlap.
n_labels <- tibble(threshold = seq(ceiling(min(thresholds) * 20) / 20, max(thresholds), by = 0.05)) |>
  mutate(n = map_int(threshold, ~ sum(by_referent$referent_r >= .x - 1e-9)))
y_min <- min(threshold_fits$ci_low, threshold_fits$mean, 0, na.rm = TRUE)

ggplot(threshold_fits, aes(x = threshold, y = mean, colour = model, fill = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ci_low, ymax = ci_high), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_label(data = n_labels, aes(x = threshold, y = y_min - 0.08, label = n),
             inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 2.6, colour = "grey30", fill = "white",
             label.size = 0, label.padding = unit(0.1, "lines")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-1, 1, 0.1)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("ToM model" = "#1E6E76", "Deductive model" = "#B8792A"), name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("ToM model" = "#1E6E76", "Deductive model" = "#B8792A"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Minimum referent correlation with ToM model",
       y = "Mean per-participant correlation\n(belief inferences)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

I also visualized within-participant correlation with each model.
```{r}
# Exploratory: can participants be split post hoc into those who reason like the ToM model and
# those who reason like the deductive model? Belief inferences only, three ways:
#
# 1. Per-participant classification. Bootstrap each participant's 14 trials (2,000 resamples,
#    keeping a trial's x and y together) for a 95% CI on their r difference; "ToM" or "deductive"
#    if the CI excludes zero, otherwise "unclear". With 14 trials and two models whose belief
#    predictions are correlated, many participants are expected to be unclear.
# 2. Held-out test of the split. Randomly split each participant's trials into halves (500
#    times), pick the better-fitting model on one half, and score it on the other. If every
#    participant really used the same strategy, choosing per participant only adds noise and
#    should not beat assigning everyone the ToM model; if some used the deductive strategy, it
#    should. Paired t test over participants of the held-out gain, averaged over splits.
#    The split-half correlation of the r difference across participants is also reported
#    (permutation p); note that it can be positive just because participants differ in how noisy
#    they are, so it shows stable differences, not necessarily two strategies.
# 3. Group comparison. Participants grouped by which model fits them better on all trials,
#    with each group's mean correlation with both models.
belief_long <- function(long) {
  long |>
    filter(startsWith(variable, "cg")) |>
    left_join(model_predictions, by = c("TrialId", "variable")) |>
    semi_join(fits_by_type(long) |> filter(type == "Belief"), by = "participant_id")
}
r_diff <- function(d) score_fit(d$response, d$ToM) - score_fit(d$response, d$Deductive)

classify_participants <- function(b, R = 2000, seed = 251) {
  set.seed(seed)
  b |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    group_modify(function(d, key) {
      rows <- split(seq_len(nrow(d)), d$TrialId)
      boots <- replicate(R, {
        s <- sample(names(rows), replace = TRUE)
        suppressWarnings(r_diff(d[unlist(rows[s]), ]))
      })
      ci <- quantile(boots, c(0.025, 0.975), na.rm = TRUE)
      tibble(diff = r_diff(d), ci_low = ci[1], ci_high = ci[2])
    }) |>
    ungroup() |>
    mutate(class = case_when(ci_low > 0 ~ "ToM", ci_high < 0 ~ "Deductive", TRUE ~ "Unclear"))
}

split_halves <- function(b, n_splits = 500, seed = 251) {
  set.seed(seed)
  b <- arrange(b, participant_id, TrialId, variable)
  ids <- split(b$TrialId, b$participant_id) |> map(unique)
  map_dfr(seq_len(n_splits), function(s) {
    h1 <- imap_dfr(ids, ~ tibble(participant_id = .y, TrialId = sample(.x, length(.x) %/% 2)))
    b |>
      mutate(half = if_else(paste(participant_id, TrialId) %in% paste(h1$participant_id, h1$TrialId),
                            "h1", "h2")) |>
      group_by(participant_id, half) |>
      summarise(a = suppressWarnings(score_fit(response, ToM)),
                d = suppressWarnings(score_fit(response, Deductive)), .groups = "drop") |>
      pivot_wider(names_from = half, values_from = c(a, d)) |>
      mutate(split = s)
  })
}

# Held-out fit of each participant's own model (chosen on the other half, both directions),
# against the ToM and deductive models for everyone; averaged over splits per participant.
held_out <- function(halves) {
  halves |>
    mutate(own_h2 = if_else(a_h1 - d_h1 >= 0, a_h2, d_h2),
           own_h1 = if_else(a_h2 - d_h2 >= 0, a_h1, d_h1)) |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(own = mean(c(own_h1, own_h2), na.rm = TRUE),
              tom = mean(c(a_h1, a_h2), na.rm = TRUE),
              ded = mean(c(d_h1, d_h2), na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
}

split_half_r <- function(halves, n_perm = 2000, seed = 251) {
  per_split <- split(halves, halves$split) |>
    map(~ list(x = .x$a_h1 - .x$d_h1, y = .x$a_h2 - .x$d_h2))
  mean_r <- function(perm) mean(map_dbl(per_split, ~ cor(.x$x, .x$y[perm], use = "complete.obs")))
  n <- length(per_split[[1]]$x)
  obs <- mean_r(seq_len(n))
  set.seed(seed)
  null <- replicate(n_perm, mean_r(sample(n)))
  tibble(r = obs, p = mean(null >= obs))
}

strategy <- map(list(Original = original_long, `Phase 1: replication` = replication_long(phase1)),
                function(long) {
                  b <- belief_long(long)
                  halves <- split_halves(b)
                  list(class = classify_participants(b), held = held_out(halves),
                       reliability = split_half_r(halves))
                })

imap_dfr(strategy, ~ .x$class |>
           count(class) |>
           mutate(class = factor(class, levels = c("ToM", "Deductive", "Unclear"))) |>
           complete(class, fill = list(n = 0)) |>
           mutate(value = sprintf("%d (%.0f%%)", n, 100 * n / sum(n))) |>
           select(class, value) |>
           pivot_wider(names_from = class, values_from = value) |>
           mutate(Study = .y, .before = 1)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Exploratory: participants whose per-participant bootstrapped 95% CI on the r difference (ToM − deductive, belief inferences) lies above zero (ToM), below zero (deductive), or includes zero (unclear).")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-strategy-split
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| fig-cap: "Exploratory: each participant's difference in correlation with the ToM and deductive models (belief inferences), with a 95% CI from bootstrapping their trials, original study and Phase 1 replication. Colour shows whether the CI lies above zero, below zero, or includes it."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
imap_dfr(strategy, ~ mutate(.x$class, Study = .y)) |>
  mutate(class = factor(class, levels = c("ToM", "Deductive", "Unclear")),
         participant = fct_reorder(paste(Study, participant_id), diff)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = diff, y = participant, colour = class)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = ci_low, xmax = ci_high), size = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ Study, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(ToM = "#1E6E76", Deductive = "#B8792A", Unclear = "grey60"),
                      name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Difference in correlation with ToM and deductive models (belief)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom")
```

I tried to replicate all of the analyses and plots from experiment 1 of the original study.
```{r}
#| label: exp1-reproduction
#| eval: !expr have_data
# The original's other Experiment 1 analyses (Exp1_AnalyzeResults.R), run on the original data
# and ours: collapsed (item-level) correlations and their difference, and the per-participant
# tests for both inference types.
items_by_study <- list(Original = item_means(original_long),
                       `Phase 1: replication` = item_means(replication_long(phase1)))
item_r  <- imap_dfr(items_by_study, ~ item_corrs(.x) |> mutate(Study = .y))
item_dr <- imap_dfr(items_by_study, ~ item_diff(.x) |> mutate(Study = .y))
subj_r  <- bind_rows(original_fits |> mutate(Study = "Original"),
                     replication_fits(phase1) |> mutate(Study = "Phase 1: replication"))

fmt_ci <- function(est, lo, hi) sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", est, lo, hi)
collapsed <- item_r |>
  filter(type != "Overall") |>
  transmute(Study, type, model, value = fmt_ci(estimate, ci_low, ci_high)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = value) |>
  left_join(item_dr |> transmute(Study, type, `ToM − deductive` = fmt_ci(estimate, ci_low, ci_high)),
            by = c("Study", "type")) |>
  mutate(Level = "Collapsed (r of item means)", `Fit ToM better` = "")
per_participant <- subj_r |>
  group_by(Study, type) |>
  summarise(tt = list(t.test(score_a, score_b, paired = TRUE)),
            a = mean(score_a), b = mean(score_b), n = n(), wins = sum(diff > 0), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(Level = "Per participant (mean r)",
         `ToM model` = sprintf("%.2f", a), `Deductive model` = sprintf("%.2f", b),
         `ToM − deductive` = map_chr(tt, ~ sprintf("%s, t(%.0f) = %.2f, p %s",
                                                   fmt_ci(.x$estimate, .x$conf.int[1], .x$conf.int[2]),
                                                   .x$parameter, .x$statistic,
                                                   if (.x$p.value < 0.001) "< 0.001"
                                                   else sprintf("= %.2g", .x$p.value))),
         `Fit ToM better` = sprintf("%d of %d (%.0f%%)", wins, n, 100 * wins / n))
bind_rows(collapsed, per_participant) |>
  mutate(Type = type) |>
  arrange(Type, desc(Level), Study) |>
  select(Type, Level, Study, `ToM model`, `Deductive model`, `ToM − deductive`, `Fit ToM better`) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Experiment 1 analyses of the original, run on the original data and on Phase 1: correlations with each model computed on item means (collapsed over participants; bootstrapped 95% CIs) and per participant (mean r; paired t test).")

item_r |>
  filter(type == "Overall") |>
  transmute(Study, model, r = fmt_ci(estimate, ci_low, ci_high)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = r) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Collapsed correlation with each model over all 168 item means (belief and referent pooled), bootstrapped 95% CIs.")
```

## Discussion

### Summary of replication attempt

In this study, I attempted to replicate Jara-Ettinger & Rubio-Fernandez (2021) that examined whether the way in which participants represent beliefs about what objects a person speaking can see can be modeled with a theory-of-mind model that accounted for the specificity of their language. Across 60 participants, the original study found that participant beliefs were more correlated with a theory-of-mind model compared to a deductive model that did not account for the specificity of speakers' language ($p$<.0001, $d$=0.70). I attempted to replicate this study across 20 participants to find the original effect with 80% power. In my replication, participants' beliefs were not differently predicted by the theory-of-mind model or the deductive model ($p$=.98, $d$=-0.01). Given the closeness of the found effect size to zero and the high p-value, my assessment was that this study failed to replicate.

### Commentary

In exploratory analyses, I attempted to replicate additional analyses that the original authors conducted and to filter participants based on additional attention checks. Interestingly, correlation with the theory-of-mind and deductive models were lower within-participant even for referent inference, a task that does not require any reasoning about how specific participants' language is. This analysis suggests that some participants may have not fully understood the task or may be satisficing and not actually answering truthfully. However, filtering to only participants who completed the comprehension check on the first try did not increase the found effect size, suggesting that additional questions may be required to fully capture participant comprehension. An exploratory analysis splitting the participants based on which model they were better predicted by did find that 9 out of 20 participants' data was better predicted by the deductive model. 

These analyses and this replication broadly might indicate that some people deploy theory-of-mind when reasoning about speaker beliefs while others do not, and that the difference between the number of people who choose either strategy may not be significant. The difference in platform, MTurk versus Prolific, is unlikely to have moderated these results, especially as participants had to complete the same comprehension check across platforms. The change in sample size could have plausibly moderated these results, reducing the power required to detect a smaller effect. 

# Phase 2: Extension

Best-practices rescue

## Rationale

There are multiple plausible reasons why Phase 1 may have not reproduced the original result. First, my sample size may have been too small to detect the true effect. I chose my original sample size so as to detect the original reported effect size which may have been inflated with 80% power, meaning I did not have enough power to detect a true smaller effect. To address this, I will choose a sample size that can detect an effect half the size of the one originally reported with 80% power. Second, participants may have not been answering truthfully all the time. For example, some participants did not move the trackpad to change the default blind spot on every trial. To address this, I will require participants to move both trackpads (to select a referent and to select a blind spot) on every trial before proceeding. Similarly, some participants may have not fully processed the utterance on each trial as indicated by the lower reference correlation compared to the original study. I will add an exclusion criterion to exclude participants whose reference correlation is lower than 0.8. 

Third, some participants may have simply adopted the less computationally intensive strategy that is captured by our deductive model. To understand if that is the case, I will add a funnel debrief at the end of the experiment where participants provide open responses about how they decided what the speakers' blind spot was and how they interpreted ambiguous naming instances. In exploratory analyses, I will measure whether participants who say they used word choice have responses that correlate more with the theory-of-mind model compared to the deductive model. Fourth, it is possible that some participants did not fully comprehend our task, especially how participants' blind spots were the same across each pair of events. To address this, I will add another question to the comprehension quiz where participants answer where the blind spot is in a second event, given the blind spot in a first event. Finally, it is possible that our key analyses, a paired t-test, is not robust enough to capture individual differences in variance. To be able to account for that variance, I plan to add an exploratory model that looks at the ELPD difference of the theory-of-mind model and the deductive model in predicting participant data.

## Changes from Phase 1


| # | Category | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sample | 20 analyzed participants | 67 analyzed participants | Phase 1's interval was too wide to distinguish the original effect from a much smaller one. |
| 2 | Trial continuation requirement | None | Participants must move all the track pads on each trial to move ahead. | Ensures participants attempt to answer truthfully on every trial even when they are guessing |
| 3 | Exclusion criteria | Completion, model fit possible | Completion, model fit possible, reference model correlation above 0.8 | Ensures participants are reading and understanding the utterances since the reference model only tests comprehension. |
| 4 | Checks | Comprehension check required to be passed | Additional question that asks participants what the blind spot across a pair of trials is | Confirms participants understand that the blind spot if the same across each pair of events. |
| 5 | Exploratory measure | None | At the end: "How did you decide where the speaker's blind spot was?" | Exploratory only; collected after every confirmatory measure. |
| 6 | Exploratory analysis | None | Measure whether ELPD predictivity is greater for the theory-of-mind model compared to the deductive model; test whether participants who report using word choice to make decisions in the task fit theory-of-mind model better | Exploratory only. |

Everything not listed above is identical to Phase 1.

## Power and sample

I chose a sample of 67 to be able to detect an effect size of 0.35, half of the original reported effect size, with 80% power. I expect that the estimate will be around the same as that as phase 1 and that the precision will higher with a confidence interval half as wide.

```{r}
#| label: phase2-power
phase2_n <- 67  # planned analysed participants in Phase 2 (each scored against both models)

p1_scores <- if (have_data) participant_scores(phase1)
p1_stats  <- if (have_data) paired_test(p1_scores)
orig      <- original_paired(original)

# SD of the per-participant differences, which sets precision. Taken from Phase 1 if it has
# data, otherwise recovered from the original's mean difference and t.
basis <- if (!is.null(p1_stats)) {
  list(sd_diff = sd(p1_scores$diff), source = "Phase 1")
} else {
  list(sd_diff = abs(original$mean_diff) * sqrt(original$n) / abs(original$t),
       source = "the original study")
}

# Expected 95% CI half-width on the mean difference with n participants.
half_width <- function(n) qt(0.975, n - 1) * basis$sd_diff / sqrt(n)
power_at <- function(n, dz) {
  tryCatch(power.t.test(n = n, delta = abs(dz), sd = 1, sig.level = 0.05,
                        type = "paired")$power,
           error = function(e) NA)
}

rows <- tibble(
  Study = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) "Phase 1 (actual)", "Phase 2 (planned)"),
  `N analysed` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) p1_stats$N, phase2_n),
  `95% CI half-width` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("±%.3f", (p1_stats$ci_high - p1_stats$ci_low) / 2),
                          sprintf("±%.3f (expected)", half_width(phase2_n)))
)
knitr::kable(rows, caption = sprintf("Precision of the key estimate (Model A minus Model B), Phase 2 expected values based on %s.", basis$source))

tibble(
  `Effect to detect` = c(sprintf("Original: d_z = %.2f", orig$d_z),
                         if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("Phase 1: d_z = %.2f", p1_stats$d_z),
                         sprintf("Half the original: d_z = %.2f", orig$d_z / 2)),
  `Power at planned N` = scales::percent(c(
    power_at(phase2_n, orig$d_z),
    if (!is.null(p1_stats)) power_at(phase2_n, p1_stats$d_z),
    power_at(phase2_n, orig$d_z / 2)
  ), accuracy = 1)
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf("Power of the Phase 2 paired t test at %d participants, two-sided alpha = .05.", phase2_n))
```

## Analysis plan

**Key analysis of interest.** Participants' performance on the belief task has a higher correlation with a theory-of-mind model as compared to a deductive model, tested with a paired t-test comparing the per-participant correlation difference. The effect size is the mean difference divided by the standard deviation of the differences, with a 95% confidence interval. I will also report a pooled estimate across phases.

In an exploratory analysis, I will also measure the ELPD difference between how the theory-of-mind model and the deductive model fit within-participant data. I will predict each participant's data using a leave-one-out trial method. I will assume that the data follows a gaussian distribution for the likelihood. For the regression, I will include random intercepts for participants and the trial id, and a by-participant random slope for the model value. I will choose loose priors, such as setting the slope to be N(0,1).
